LS5034 Cardiovascular Physiology Practical

Safety and eligibility:
Anyone suffering from or having a history of high blood pressure, heart disease or peripheral vascular disease should not volunteer to carry out these experiments. 
Anyone with any other medical condition please speak to the academic before volunteering. 
Anyone on any medication please speak to academic before volunteering.
Anyone with skin conditions or open wounds (in hand) should not volunteer
Anyone prone to dizziness or fainting should not volunteer
Pregnant or breast feeding females should not volunteer
You MUST all have read the risk assessment document before coming to lab.
You MUST read and sign the consent form before participating as a volunteer in the practical.

Learning outcomes:

Accurate execution of a physiological experiment involving accurate measuring of physiological parameters such as blood pressure 
Understanding of haemodynamics including factors that determine blood pressure and relationship between blood pressure and blood flow
Understanding the physiological mechanisms underlying the experimental observations 
Interpretation of results, including understanding of methods and sources of error


Experiments: 
1) The effect of ambient temperature on arterial blood pressure 
2) The effect of recovery from ischemia on arterial blood pressure

The ability to determine cardiovascular variables such as blood pressure, heart rate, blood flow and cardiac output is essential in determining both an individual’s fitness and health.  Arterial blood pressure, can easily be measured without the need for invasive techniques and blood pressure can give us an indication of blood flow.  

Ambient temperature and ischaemia can both alter blood flow. Measurement of  BP can tell us about blood flow and factors affecting blood flow.  

Blood pressure is a variable that is determined by cardiac output and total peripheral resistance 
   mean arterial pressure = cardiac output X total peripheral resistance. 
                               (MAP=CO X TPR)

We can infer what may be happening to blood flow by observing whether
BP decreases or increases.  Total peripheral resistance (TPR) which reflects the resistance to blood flow from all blood vessels, can be controlled by altering blood vessel diameter/radius (vasoconstriction or vasodilatation), and has a direct influence on peripheral blood flow. Flow will increase as blood vessels dilate.  This decreases resistance to flow and therefore will decrease blood pressure also.  In these experiments, arterial blood pressure will be measured by use of an electronic blood pressure monitor.

Heart rate can be measured by simple palpation at the wrist on the radial artery or using the electronic BP monitor.  


Aims of the Experiments

To determine the effect of temperature on arterial blood pressure and by inference, peripheral blood flow.
To determine the effect of recovery from ischaemia on arterial blood pressure, and by inference, peripheral blood flow.
  
Experiment 1: 
Effect of Ambient Temperature on Arterial Pressure.

Apparatus: hot water, ice, thermometer, blood pressure monitor, stopwatch
You will undertake these experiments working in groups of 5-6.

In this experiment you will determine the relationship between ambient (surrounding) temperature and arterial blood pressure.  The experiment is comprised of two parts, part 1 investigating effect of low (below body temp) temperature, part 2 investigating effect of high (above body temp) temperature.  A different person in each group should act as the subject for the first and second parts.

Part 1: Effect of cold water on BP (Cold pressor Test (CPT)):

Into the bucket/box provided, mix ice with tap water to achieve a temperature of       5-60C. Make sure you stir well to distribute the temperature evenly.  Use the thermometer provided to make sure the temperature is 5-60C. Temperature must NOT be below 40C. Do NOT put hand directly in solid ice.

Subject should sit down and relax.  Place the blood pressure monitor cuff around the  upper arm, record systolic (SBP) & diastolic (DBP) BP to obtain an initial baseline reading.  Take a minimum of 2 readings and calculate the mean. The BP monitor will also give the pulse rate, record this as well on the proforma. 

The subject must then quietly rest for 2 minutes.

Then immerse the hand in cold water at  ~5-60C to just cover up to the wrist for 1.5 minutes only. Make sure you do NOT keep your hand in cold water for more than 2 minutes. 
If it is too painful or uncomfortable at any time please remove hand immediately and wipe dry.

30 seconds after immersion, record systolic and diastolic BP and HR and continue to measure BP at 30sec intervals whilst the hand is still immersed.. 
After 1.5 minutes, remove hand from cold water. Immediately measure systolic and diastolic BPs and the pulse rate at 30s intervals until BP and pulse have returned to normal. 
You should have 3 BP reading whilst the hand is in the cold water and 3 reading after hand has been removed.

CPT is used to measure BP reactivity to cold stress, and previous studies have shown that increased BP response to CPT is associated with greater risk of developing hypertension. 
(reference: Kasagi et al., 1995. Relation between Cold Pressor test and development of hypertension based on 28 year follow-up. Hypertension 25, 71-76). 

Part 2: Effect of hot water on BP:
Set a tub of hot water at 450C-460C  by mixing hot water from kettle with tap water. Stir well to get an even temperature throughout the container. Make sure the temperature is NOT above 470C.

Repeat the experiment as above (a different subject should volunteer) using hot water. Do not keep hand in hot water for more than 2 minutes.

If it is too painful or uncomfortable at any time please remove hand immediately and wipe dry or hold under running cool water.

While the hand is placed in the water note any changes in skin colour and if there is any pooling of venous blood (pooling can occur as a consequence of increased blood flow and is seen as an increase in surface blood vessel size – this happens as the veins are thin walled and easily distensible).

Answer the following questions:
1. Calculate the mean systolic and diastolic BPs obtained before immersion. 

2. For the cold water test, calculate the largest BP change (subtract the mean initial/baseline pressures from the highest reading obtained during or after immersion).

3. What are the mechanisms behind the arterial pressure changes that were observed (or you think should have been observed) in response to changes in ambient temperature?  Consider both local and systemic mechanisms.  
4. 
Did you observe if either the hot or cold water had any effect on pooling of venous blood in the immersed hand?  (if so does this correspond with what you think may happen?).

What factors may affect the blood pressure response to the Cold Pressor Test? Zhang M et al., American Journal of Hypertension. 2013. Volume 26(9), 1132-1139).

If systolic BP increases by 25 mmHg or more or if diastolic BP increases by 20 mmHg or more they are considered to be hyper-reactive. (Reference:  Wood DL, Sheps SG, Elveback LR, Schirger A. Cold pressor test is a predictor of hypertension. Hypertension 6: 301–306, 1984).
Kasagi  et al., Relation between cold pressor test and development of hypertension based on 28 year follow up. Hypertension. 1995 25(1):71-76.


Experiment 2: 
Effect of Ischaemia on Peripheral Circulation.

Apparatus: inflatable sphygmomanometer cuff, electronic blood pressure monitor, stopwatch

This experiment will explore reactive hyperaemia (post-ischaemic hyperaemia). Reactive Hyperaemia is the temporary, increase in blood flow to a tissue, that occurs after a period of blood flow occlusion (ischaemia).

The aim of this experiment is to investigate change in blood pressure (by inference blood flow) during recovery from ischaemia by:
a) inducing reversible ischaemia (lack of oxygen) in the forearm by compressing blood vessels supplying the forearm 
b) recording blood pressure once normal blood supply has been re-established (during recovery from ischaemia).   


Experimental procedure:
Measure your resting blood pressure using the electronic blood pressure monitor. Take at least 2 baseline blood pressure readings. Calculate mean systolic and diastolic BP. Keep the cuff on the arm for the duration of the experiment.
If your resting systolic BP is above 130 mmHg you should speak to the academic before taking part in the experiment.
Place the manual sphygmomanometer cuff around the other arm (not the arm used to measure blood pressure) (note; the manual sphygmomanometer cuff is being used to make the forearm ischaemic, NOT to measure blood pressure).

Inflate the manual cuff to 20 mmHg above the measured resting systolic BP. This would compress the blood vessels supplying the forearm. You must NOT inflate the cuff above 150 mmHg.  Keep the manual cuff inflated for 30 seconds ONLY. 
 NB: If at any point pain/discomfort or numbness/tingling is felt, STOP and release the pressure in the manual cuff immediately and remove the cuff.



After30 seconds, remove the manual cuff and immediately record blood pressure using the automatic BP monitor on the other arm.  Repeat measurements at 30 second intervals for a 3 minute period.  Also note if there are any changes in skin colour occurring during this recovery period.
